sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Scota was an Irish heroine and a vague figure in Irish legend. The Book of Invasions called her a daughter of the pharaoh Cingris, blending ancient Irish lore with biblical legend. Another woman of the same name was also called a pharaoh's daughter, this time of Nechtanebus. She was the wife of Míl, the wandering soldier whose children, the Milesians, were held to be the ancestors of the Irish. Scota may have been a Celtic ancestor goddess, for the people of Ireland were once called scoti, a name that later stuck in another Celtic homeland, Scotland. The tale joins an Egyptian princess to the origin story of the Gaels and gives the Irish a royal descent.
